bullets: ‘Double, double toil and trouble; / Fire burn, and cauldron bubble’: **trochaic tetrameter** and rhyming couplets set the Witches apart from human characters’ iambic verse: an incantation.
Revolting ingredients (‘Eye of newt’, ‘Finger of birth-strangled babe’): the Jacobean audience’s fear of witchcraft.
‘By the pricking of my thumbs, / Something wicked this way comes’: Macbeth is now ‘wicked’ even to witches.
Apparition 2, a **bloody child**: ‘none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth’: **equivocation**; Macduff was born by caesarean.
Apparition 3, a **crowned child holding a tree**: Macbeth will not be vanquished until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane.
The **show of eight kings** with Banquo’s ghost holding a mirror: Banquo’s descendants as kings, flattering James I.
‘From this moment / The very firstlings of my heart shall be / The firstlings of my hand’: he will act on impulse without thought: tyranny.
He resolves to ‘give to th’ edge o’ th’ sword’ Macduff’s ‘wife, his babes’: violence against innocents.

callouts.p: Each prophecy is true but misleading. Link to the Porter’s ‘equivocator’ and the Gunpowder Plot trials: double meanings lead to damnation.

core.h: Act 4 Scene 1: the cauldron and the apparitions
core.p: The Witches chant over their cauldron. Macbeth demands answers and sees three apparitions and a show of eight kings.

bullets: ‘He loves us not; / He wants the natural touch’: she believes Macduff has failed as a husband and father.
The witty dialogue with her son creates **pathos**: an ordinary, loving family.
‘Whither should I fly? / I have done no harm’: innocence in a world where evil rules.
The son’s murder on stage: Macbeth’s tyranny reaches its lowest point. Contrast Lady Macbeth’s imagined infanticide in 1.7.
core.p: Lady Macduff, abandoned by her husband who has fled to England, talks with her son. Murderers arrive and kill them both.

bullets: Malcolm lists the **‘king-becoming graces’**: justice, verity, temperance, stableness, bounty, perseverance, mercy, lowliness, devotion, patience, courage, fortitude. A model of good kingship, the opposite of Macbeth.
Macduff: ‘O Scotland, Scotland!’: patriotism; his grief for the country convinces Malcolm.
The English king (Edward the Confessor) can **heal** the sick by touch: the holy king contrasted with the tyrant.
‘All my pretty ones? / Did you say all? O hell-kite! All?’: broken questions and repetition of ‘all’; Macbeth as a bird of prey.

Malcolm: ‘Dispute it like a man.’ Macduff: ‘I shall do so; / But I must also feel it as a man’: **redefines masculinity** to include feeling: the play’s answer to Lady Macbeth’s ‘When you durst do it, then you were a man’.
Grief turns to ‘the whetstone of your sword’: revenge is now just.
core.p: In England, Malcolm tests Macduff’s loyalty by pretending to be worse than Macbeth. Satisfied, he reveals his true virtue. Ross brings news of the slaughter.

model: Broken questions and repetition: grief overwhelms
Macduff’s ‘feel it as a man’: redefinition
Contrast (in part b) with Lady Macbeth’s definition in 1.7
exam.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents masculinity in this extract (Act 4 Scene 3, Macduff hears the news). (20 marks)
exam.tip: Contrast definitions of manhood across the play.

mistakes.r: He is testing Macduff; he then reveals his virtue.
mistakes.w: Malcolm is really as wicked as he claims.

mistakes.r: Present Lady Macduff’s view, but note he fled to save Scotland; his grief and revenge redeem him.
mistakes.w: Macduff is a coward for leaving his family.

The very firstlings of my heart shall be / The firstlings of my hand

quotes.a: Feeling is part of true manhood.
quotes.q: I must also feel it as a man

quotes.a: A list of ideal kingly virtues.
quotes.c: Divine right; James I’s Basilikon Doron

summary: Act 4 contains the Witches’ apparitions (4.1), the murder of Lady Macduff and her son (4.2) and the England scene where Malcolm tests Macduff and Macduff learns of his family’s death (4.3): learn the key lines on the supernatural, tyranny, kingship and masculinity.

terms.d: Using ambiguous language to mislead without technically lying.
Four stressed–unstressed beats; the Witches’ chant rhythm.
Evoking pity, as in the murder of Lady Macduff’s son.
